item.title: TED: a global temperature-driven thermoelastic displacement dataset for GNSS reference stations (2000–2023)
item.category: Earth System Science Data Current Issue
item.description:
Ran Lu, Zhao Li, Lingfeng Ye, Peng Yuan, Yanming Feng
Earth System Science Data, vol. 18, issue 10, pp. 7575-7591
DOI: 10.5194/essd-18-7575-2026
Nonlinear variations in GNSS station height time series include contributions from non-tidal mass loading and temperature-driven thermoelastic displacement (TED). However, a globally consistent station-level TED product has not been widely available. Here we present a global dataset of vertical TED for approximately 14 000 GNSS stations over 2000–2023, generated using a full-spectrum layered finite-element model. The model is driven by hourly ERA5 soil-temperature forcing and parameterized with SoilGrids-derived depth-dependent subsurface properties, allowing within-day temperature variability to be incorporated into daily TED time series that retain seasonal and nonseasonal components. For the 2612 stations with documented foundation-depth information, site-information-constrained solutions agree closely with SoilGrids-based solutions, with annual-amplitude differences mostly about 0.01–0.03 mm and annual-phase differences generally within 1–3°. Sensitivity tests using ± 10 % perturbations in the linear thermal expansion coefficient, thermal diffusivity, and Young's modulus indicate that the amplitude and phase of the annual TED component are stable under reasonable parameter uncertainty. Globally, annual TED amplitudes are mostly within about 0.2–1.2 mm and locally exceed 1.5 mm, with larger signals concentrated in arid inland and continental regions. The percentile-based peak-to-peak variability of the full daily TED series commonly reaches 2–4 mm and locally approaches 5–6 mm. When applied alone to GNSS height time series, TED produces positive WRMS reductions at about 79 % of the assessed stations, with most improvements within 3 %–5 % and the largest reductions reaching about 10 %. The dataset is publicly available for direct use in GNSS height time series correction and related geophysical applications: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21069958 (Lu et al., 2026a).

item.title: High-resolution global groundwater storage anomalies: a 1 km downscaled dataset
item.category: Earth System Science Data Current Issue
item.description:
Chen Zhang, Yifei Fan, Wenxia Han, Yingchun Ge, Jiabei Zhu, Tao Che
Earth System Science Data, vol. 18, issue 10, pp. 7593-7626
DOI: 10.5194/essd-18-7593-2026
Groundwater depletion poses a challenge to water security, but the coarse spatial resolution of Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment (GRACE) observations limits the characterization of groundwater variability at regional and local scales. Here, we present a 1 km monthly global groundwater storage anomaly (GWSA) dataset covering April 2002–December 2020. The dataset was generated using Singular Spectrum Analysis (SSA) for temporal gap filling, 19 high-resolution hydroclimatic and geophysical predictors, and aquifer-stratified machine-learning downscaling. Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) and deep neural networks (DNN) were evaluated as candidate models, and XGBoost was selected for dataset production based on internal, cross-scale, and in-situ evaluations. When aggregated to the original GRACE scale, the 1 km product agreed closely with the original GWSA ( R 2 = 0.972, RMSE = 2.10 cm). Independent evaluation used a global archive of 152 069 groundwater-monitoring wells and a 1° spatial-block calibration–validation design. Effective specific yield ( S yeff ) was estimated from calibration blocks and transferred to held-out blocks before comparison at a common 0.25° grid. For XGBoost, the held-out evaluation yielded R 2 = 0.538, RMSE = 0.378 cm yr −1 , and Bias = 0.106 cm yr −1 . The association between modeled and observation-derived trends remained similar under ± 30 % perturbations in S yeff , although amplitude-related metrics were more sensitive to the conversion coefficient. Standardized time-series comparisons and monthly evaluations of representative aquifers showed better agreement for long-term variability than for seasonal variability. Comparisons with published regional estimates showed close agreement in the North China Plain, weaker depletion magnitudes in northwestern India and California, and a trend-sign mismatch in the High Plains Aquifer during 2003–2013. Experiments using CSR, JPL, H08, and WaterGAP also showed that reconstruction performance and predictor importance depend on the target product. The dataset provides kilometre-scale estimates of groundwater-storage variability under the large-scale GRACE constraint. Local interpretation of the reconstructed spatial patterns requires additional groundwater-level, abstraction, and hydrogeological observations. The 1 km monthly global GWSA dataset is openly available from the National Cryosphere Desert Data Center at https://doi.org/10.12072/ncdc.hydrology.db7323.2026 (Fan et al., 2026).
